The lighthouse keeper had not spoken to another person in eleven days. He kept a
log of the weather, the ships that passed, and the condition of the lamp, and on
the twelfth morning he noticed that he had started writing the entries as though
someone else would read them. "Wind from the north-east, moderate," he wrote,
and then, after a pause, "You would have liked the light this morning."

It was not loneliness exactly. The work filled the hours: the brass needed
polishing, the clockwork that turned the lens needed winding every four hours,
and the stairs (one hundred and twelve of them) needed sweeping because the
salt got into everything. But the work did not talk back, and he found that he
had begun to narrate it, quietly, to an audience of gulls.

When the supply boat finally came, the young woman who brought the crates asked
him how he was. He opened his mouth to answer and found that he had forgotten
how short a reply is supposed to be. He told her about the wind, and the lamp,
and the gulls, and the ships, and when he finished she was smiling and the tide
had turned. She said she would come back on Thursday. He wrote that down, too.

Most of what we call patience is simply the habit of not counting. The keeper
stopped counting the days after that, and the log grew shorter, and the light
went round and round above the water the way it always had, for anyone who
happened to be looking.
